title: Field meal allowance audit
text:
The question
Fiorena’s financial control team saw the meal allowance paid per crew-day in the field rise from R$ 219 in the first half of 2025 to R$ 239 in the second, 9.5% more, with no change in the allowance amounts or in the type of work. The question was simple: how much of that is legitimate spending, and how much was paid outside the rules?










Meal allowance paid per crew-day in the field, month by month, in 2025. The dashed line is the same amount without what the audit classified as improper. The mark in August is the switch to a new top-up system.















Meal allowance paid per crew-day in the field, month by month, in 2025. The dashed line is the same amount without what the audit classified as improper. The mark in August is the switch to a new top-up system.





The July dip has a cause in the data: July and January are the months with the most people on vacation (in July, 81 lineworkers per business day, against 37 in the median month), and each crew went out with 3.5 people, against 3.8 in the median. The amount per person in the field did not fall: it stayed between R$ 58 and R$ 60 from January to July.
Each lineworker gets one top-up on their meal card per day in the field. The base enters the top-up, the supervisor approves it, and it is paid with no automatic check against the field log or the vacation and leave records. Nobody had looked at all 12 months of records together.
The audit answered three questions, in this order:

How much was paid outside an objective rule (duplicates, over the cap, people who were not working)?
How much was paid with no support: no record of the crew in the field that day, or a justification that explains nothing?
Where is it concentrated, and why?

title: Field meal allowance audit
text:
The rule and the data
The allowance rule:

Lunch of R$ 52 per day in the field.
Dinner of R$ 44, only when the field log records an overnight stay for the crew.
Extra of up to R$ 24, only with one of the listed justifications: “travel of more than 300 km” or “workday extended by more than 2 hours”.
Cap of R$ 120 per person per day, all included, and at most one top-up of each type per day.
Only for people who are active, not on vacation or leave, and on a crew that was in the field that day.

The audit covered 155,909 top-ups from 2025, totaling R$ 7.63 million, paid to 649 people at 8 bases, cross-checked against 33,254 crew-in-the-field records in the log, the HR roster, and HR’s vacation and leave records.

title: Field meal allowance audit
text:
Method
Every top-up goes through the same checks and ends up in one of four conclusions. The audit separates objective errors, which can be recovered, from what only deserves a second look from the base; it draws no conclusion about anyone’s intent.

Prepare. Use the day worked, not the date the top-up was entered, and link each top-up to the HR roster, to leave records and to the person’s crew that day.
Check the objective rules. Duplicates, person not on duty, dinner with no overnight stay, extra with no justification, and a daily total over the cap. For the cap, only the excess counts as improper.
Check the support. Was the crew in the field that day? Is the justification for the extra valid, vague or missing? A term dictionary tolerates typos, so that “deslocamneto acima de 300km” (misspelled, in Portuguese) still counts as valid.
Compare with what is expected. For each base and month, the amount per field day is compared with the other bases in the same month. A group falls outside the expected range when it strays much further than bases usually stray from one another (Tukey’s criterion, in the code).
Score the risk. One point for each signal: rule broken, no field record, vague or missing justification, base and month above the range.
Conclude. Each top-up gets one of the four conclusions below.













Conclusion
When
What to do




Improper
Broke an objective rule
Reverse or recover, according to company policy and with support from HR and legal


Review
No rule broken, but no field record, or two signals or more
The base confirms or corrects it within 15 days


Watch
A single signal, no rule broken
Goes into next month’s sample


Compliant
No signal
Nothing to do

Show the R code for step 1: prepare
# O que vale é o dia de referência (o dia trabalhado), e não a data em que a
# recarga foi lançada. Cada recarga é ligada ao cadastro, às ausências e à
# equipe da pessoa naquele dia no diário de campo.
recargas <- read_csv("dados/recargas.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE, na = "",
                     col_types = cols(justificativa = "c"))
diario <- read_csv("dados/diario_campo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cadastro <- read_csv("dados/cadastro.csv", show_col_types = FALSE, na = "")
ausencias <- read_csv("dados/ausencias.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

base_auditoria <- recargas |>
  mutate(dia = dia_referencia) |>
  left_join(cadastro |> select(matricula, equipe, admissao, desligamento), "matricula") |>
  left_join(ausencias |> select(matricula, tipo_ausencia = tipo, inicio, fim),
            join_by(matricula, between(dia, inicio, fim))) |>
  left_join(diario |> transmute(equipe, dia = data, em_campo = TRUE, pernoite = pernoite == "sim"),
            c("equipe", "dia")) |>
  mutate(em_campo = coalesce(em_campo, FALSE))




Show the R code for step 2: objective rules
# Regras objetivas: cada violação pode ser cobrada. No teto, só o excedente
# conta como indevido; ele é calculado depois de tirar o que já é indevido por
# outra regra, para não contar o mesmo real duas vezes.
normalizar <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(iconv(coalesce(x, ""), to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"))
  x <- gsub("([0-9])\\s*km", "\\1 km", x)
  x <- gsub("([0-9])\\s*h\\b", "\\1 horas", x)
  trimws(gsub("[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", gsub("\\s+", " ", x)))
}
# Dicionário com tolerância a erro de digitação: a justificativa vale se
# estiver a até 15% de distância (em letras) de uma das frases da regra.
classificar_justificativa <- function(x) {
  n <- normalizar(x)
  validas <- normalizar(JUSTIFICATIVAS_VALIDAS)
  dist <- adist(n, validas, partial = FALSE) / outer(nchar(n), nchar(validas), pmax)
  case_when(n == "" ~ "ausente",
            apply(dist, 1, min) <= 0.15 ~ "válida",
            TRUE ~ "vaga")
}

# Cada texto diferente é classificado uma vez só.
textos <- unique(coalesce(base_auditoria$justificativa[base_auditoria$tipo == "Extra"], ""))
classes <- classificar_justificativa(textos)

auditada <- base_auditoria |>
  mutate(justificativa_classe = if_else(tipo == "Extra", classes[match(coalesce(justificativa, ""), textos)], NA)) |>
  arrange(matricula, dia, tipo, data_recarga, id) |>
  group_by(matricula, dia, tipo) |>
  mutate(duplicidade = row_number() > 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    fora_do_trabalho = dia < admissao | (!is.na(desligamento) & dia > desligamento) | !is.na(tipo_ausencia),
    jantar_sem_pernoite = tipo == "Jantar" & !coalesce(pernoite, FALSE),
    extra_sem_justificativa = tipo == "Extra" & justificativa_classe == "ausente",
    motivo_regra = case_when(duplicidade ~ "Duplicidade",
                             fora_do_trabalho ~ "Pessoa fora do trabalho",
                             jantar_sem_pernoite ~ "Jantar sem pernoite",
                             extra_sem_justificativa ~ "Extra sem justificativa"),
    valor_indevido = if_else(is.na(motivo_regra), 0, valor)
  )

# Teto diário: soma do que não é indevido por outra regra; o excedente sai
# primeiro do extra, depois do jantar.
ordem_corte <- c("Extra" = 1, "Jantar" = 2, "Almoço" = 3)
auditada <- auditada |>
  mutate(restante = valor - valor_indevido, corte = ordem_corte[tipo]) |>
  group_by(matricula, dia) |>
  mutate(excedente_dia = pmax(sum(restante) - TETO, 0)) |>
  arrange(corte, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(antes = cumsum(restante) - restante,
         acima_do_teto = pmin(restante, pmax(excedente_dia - antes, 0))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(valor_indevido = valor_indevido + acima_do_teto,
         motivo_regra = if_else(is.na(motivo_regra) & acima_do_teto > 0, "Acima do teto", motivo_regra),
         regra = !is.na(motivo_regra)) |>
  select(-restante, -corte, -excedente_dia, -antes)




Show the R code for step 3: support
# A equipe estava em campo naquele dia? A justificativa do extra é válida,
# vaga ou ausente?
auditada <- auditada |>
  mutate(sem_lastro = !em_campo,
         justificativa_fraca = tipo == "Extra" & justificativa_classe %in% c("vaga", "ausente"))




Show the R code for step 4: expected range
# Valor pago por dia de equipe em campo, por base e mês. Como o nível geral
# muda de um mês para outro (mais pernoites no segundo semestre), cada base é
# comparada com a mediana das bases no mesmo mês; a faixa esperada desse
# índice vem do critério de Tukey sobre todos os grupos com pelo menos 15 dias
# de equipe em campo. Como a auditoria procura pagamento a mais, só ficar
# acima da faixa conta como sinal de risco; abaixo dela, o grupo só é anotado.
dias_campo <- diario |>
  mutate(mes = format(data, "%Y-%m")) |>
  count(base, mes, name = "dias_equipe")
base_mes <- auditada |>
  mutate(mes = format(dia, "%Y-%m")) |>
  group_by(base, mes) |>
  summarise(valor = sum(valor), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(dias_campo, c("base", "mes")) |>
  mutate(valor_dia = valor / dias_equipe) |>
  group_by(mes) |>
  mutate(mediana_mes = median(valor_dia), indice = valor_dia / mediana_mes) |>
  ungroup()
validos <- base_mes |> filter(dias_equipe >= 15)
q <- quantile(validos$indice, c(0.25, 0.75))
faixa <- c(q[[1]] - 1.5 * diff(q), q[[2]] + 1.5 * diff(q))
base_mes <- base_mes |>
  mutate(faixa_min = faixa[1] * mediana_mes, faixa_max = faixa[2] * mediana_mes,
         abaixo_da_faixa = dias_equipe >= 15 & indice < faixa[1],
         fora_da_faixa = dias_equipe >= 15 & indice > faixa[2])
auditada <- auditada |>
  mutate(mes = format(dia, "%Y-%m")) |>
  left_join(base_mes |> select(base, mes, fora_da_faixa), c("base", "mes")) |>
  mutate(fora_da_faixa = coalesce(fora_da_faixa, FALSE))




Show the R code for step 5: risk score
# Um ponto para cada sinal, de 0 a 4.
auditada <- auditada |>
  mutate(score = regra + sem_lastro + justificativa_fraca + fora_da_faixa,
         score_sem_regra = score - regra)




Show the R code for step 6: conclusion
# Indevido: violou uma regra objetiva. Revisar: sem regra violada, mas sem
# lastro de campo ou com score de 2 ou mais. Atenção: score 1. Regular: 0.
# Numa recarga que passou do teto só em parte, o excedente é Indevido e o
# resto recebe a conclusão que teria sem essa regra.
concluir <- function(sem_lastro, score) {
  case_when(sem_lastro | score >= 2 ~ "Revisar", score == 1 ~ "Atenção", TRUE ~ "Regular")
}
auditada <- auditada |>
  mutate(conclusao = if_else(regra, "Indevido", concluir(sem_lastro, score)),
         conclusao_resto = concluir(sem_lastro, score_sem_regra),
         valor_resto = valor - valor_indevido)
NIVEIS <- c("Indevido", "Revisar", "Atenção", "Regular")

text:
Results
Of the amount paid in the year, R$ 305 thousand (4.0%) was improper, and another R$ 235 thousand (3.1%) needs confirmation from the base.










The amount paid in 2025, split into the audit’s four conclusions.















The amount paid in 2025, split into the audit’s four conclusions.






Improper is what broke an objective rule and can be recovered.
Review is made up almost entirely of top-ups with no field record: R$ 234 thousand in 4,500 top-ups entered on days when the crew does not appear in the log. It may be a gap in the log rather than in the top-up; that is why the base confirms before anything is recovered.
Watch is not an accusation. Of the 8,686 top-ups in Watch, 7,925 are there only because their base and month were above the expected range; the top-up itself follows the rule. Among them are 1,072 records that only looked like errors (entered one or two days late, overnight stay logged late, justification with a typo). The other 872 have a vague justification, such as “ajuste” (adjustment) or “conforme combinado” (as agreed).


Improper payments by type of defect










Improper amount in 2025 by type of defect. For the cap, only the excess over the daily limit.















Improper amount in 2025 by type of defect. For the cap, only the excess over the daily limit.







What explains the jump in the second half
The amount per field day rose by R$ 20.86. Of that increase, R$ 10.21 (49%) came from improper payments. Another R$ 8.51 (41%) came from more legitimate dinners, because overnight stays went from 11.5% to 16.8% of field days. The remaining R$ 2.14 came from the extras that come with overnight stays.

title: Field meal allowance audit
text:
Where and why

The August system switch created duplicates. Through July they add up to R$ 6 thousand; from August to December, R$ 112 thousand. The new system accepts two top-ups of the same type for the same person on the same day.
The HR roster arrives late. Of the top-ups paid to people on vacation, 100% fell in the first five days of the vacation period: the base only learns about the vacation after it has started.
Two bases pay dinner with no overnight stay. Base 3 and Base 6 account for 100% of dinners with no overnight stay, and they are the only bases with months above the expected range: 3 months at the first and 3 at the second.

section: How we know the audit got it right
text:
How we know the audit got it right
Because the data for this case were generated by a script, the audit could be checked against what the generator planted: it found all 12,905 planted defects, and none of the 19,885 records that only looked like errors ended up as Improper or Review. The audit does not read the answer key; a separate script compares the two at the end. Real data have no answer key, and that check is done with the base: a sample of cases from each conclusion is reviewed with people who know the process before the report is closed.

What this case demonstrates

Cross-checking sources nobody cross-checked. The error was not in any single source, but in the lack of checks between the card, the field log and HR.
Separating objective errors from suspicion. Only what breaks a rule goes to recovery; the rest goes back to the base to confirm, without accusing anyone.
A number that explains the problem. The jump in the second half was split into what is improper and what is legitimate, instead of turning into a blanket order to cut costs.
A report that can be rerun. The code stays with the company, and the same report runs the following year with new data.

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
The problem
A logistics operator with four distribution centers and about 1,250 people tracked absenteeism with a single monthly number. Over two years it did not move: 3.77% in 2024 and 3.77% in 2025. As far as leadership was concerned, the issue was under control.
Operations managers disagreed. They talked about more overtime to cover night-shift absences and more accidents among new hires. The number was right, and so was the perception; what was missing was a way to see both at once.

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
What the dashboard showed

The stability was arithmetic. The end of an infectious disease outbreak and fewer long-term absences offset an 8% rise in all other short-term absences.
The rise had an address. In two night-shift teams at the Duque de Caxias site, one in Picking and one in Shipping (Separação e Expedição), the short-term rate went from 3.5% to 6.5% starting in April 2025. The rest of that site and the night shift at the other sites did not change. Both teams had changed supervisors a few weeks earlier: a lead worth investigating, not a conclusion.
The night shift has a higher rate across the whole company (adjusted rate ratio of 1.31), and new hires are absent 1.8 times as often.
A few events account for many hours: 1.6% of events make up 34% of lost hours.
One apparent association was spurious. Large teams seemed to have more absences, but the only very large team worked nights. Once you split by shift, the effect disappears.

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
How it was built
The data. Thirteen tables in the export format of a Brazilian ERP: pseudonymized records for 1,826 people, scheduled hours for every day (662 thousand rows) and 13.6 thousand absence events. Recording each day’s scheduled hours is what makes it possible to calculate the rate in hours and handle late arrivals, part-time schedules, vacations and mid-month hires correctly. I also injected 146 typical extraction defects (duplicates, reversed dates, orphan keys, inconsistent spellings) so the data cleaning had something concrete to solve.
The cleaning. 26 Power Query queries clean and validate the data. One dashboard page shows what was fixed and how much, so readers know whether they can trust the numbers.
The model. A star schema with three fact tables at different grains (scheduled hours, absence per day and absence event) and 97 DAX measures, organized by topic.
The statistics. Three choices define the project:

Break it down before comparing. The total rate is always split into short-term (up to 15 days, the part a line manager can influence) and long-term (absences managed by occupational health).
Require evidence before raising an alarm. An area is flagged as critical only if the deviation is large and statistically consistent (z-score of event frequency). A six-person team with one long absence does not trigger an alert.
Test the obvious associations. A negative binomial model, adjusted for site, department, shift, age, sex, tenure and year, separated what holds up (night shift, tenure, site) from what does not (team size, sex).

The report as code. A single specification describes every visual (position, fields, measures and the question it answers). From it, a Python script generated the first version of the report, in Power BI’s project format, along with the documentation and the wireframes. The dashboard was then refined in Power BI Desktop. An audit script still checks that every measure used exists in the model and that every number quoted matches the data.
Privacy as a requirement. No names, national ID numbers or email addresses; health reasons only in aggregate; groups smaller than 10 people suppressed; row-level security by site and by manager; and an explicit note that the dashboard is not meant for disciplinary use.

title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
text:
You have probably seen this play out. The year closes, the absenteeism rate comes in the same as the year before, someone writes “stable” in the report and the topic drops off the agenda. It makes sense: if the number did not change, why spend time on it?
Because a number that stands still can be the sum of things moving in opposite directions.
In the Absenteeism Radar, a dashboard I built for a fictional company, the rate went from 3.772% in 2024 to 3.774% in 2025. A difference of two thousandths of a percentage point. If the report stopped there, the conclusion would be “nothing changed.” But quite a lot did.

title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
section: Separate what managers control from what they do not
text:
Separate what managers control from what they do not
The first step is to split the rate into two parts:

short-term: absences of up to 15 days, such as unexcused absences, short doctor’s notes and late arrivals. This is the part that day-to-day line managers can influence;
long-term: absences of more than 15 days, which occupational health usually follows case by case.

Once you split it, “stable” falls apart. Short-term absence rose 0.055 percentage points (from 2.45% to 2.51%). Long-term absence fell by almost exactly as much, 0.052 points (from 1.32% to 1.27%). One canceled out the other.

title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
text:
Then look inside short-term absence
You can dig deeper still. In 2024 there was an infectious disease outbreak between February and May, which inflated short-term absences that year. In 2025 the outbreak did not come back, and that group of reasons fell 0.113 points.
In other words, short-term absence only avoided a bigger rise because the previous year had been unusual. Take infectious diseases out of the count and all other short-term absences rose 0.17 percentage points, an 8% increase.

title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
section: What I would do about it
text:
What I would do about it
Two simple changes to how this gets reported:

Use the short-term rate as a management KPI for line managers. It is the rate that responds to supervision, scheduling and onboarding of new hires.
Never present the total rate on its own. Always break it down into short-term and long-term, ideally with the main groups of reasons alongside.

title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
text:
A word of caution
Breaking the rate down shows where the change comes from, not why it happened. Knowing that short-term absence rose 8% outside infectious diseases is the start of the investigation, not the end. In the Radar case, the next step showed that the rise was concentrated in two night-shift teams; but that is a topic for another post.
If you track absenteeism at your company, the exercise is worth it: take the rate for the last two years and split it into short-term and long-term. Your “stable” may be hiding something too.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
text:
July 2025, the monthly results meeting. The agenda asked for something simple: understand the June absenteeism rate. HR opened its presentation with 4.38%. Operations, right after, showed 3.54%. Finance had 2.15% in the spreadsheet that went around before the meeting. Three departments, the same month, the same KPI and three different numbers.
Much of the meeting went into trying to figure out which one was right. Nobody left with a decision about absenteeism. They left with a task, “align the numbers,” before the next meeting, where the scene played out again.
The scene comes from a demo case in my portfolio, built on fictional data. But anyone who has sat through a results meeting will probably recognize it.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
section: The cost nobody puts in the spreadsheet
text:
The cost nobody puts in the spreadsheet
A KPI with three versions never shows up as an expense anywhere, so it tends to be treated as a minor annoyance. But it is expensive, in several ways at once.
It costs the time of expensive people: directors and managers arguing about where the number came from instead of what to do about it. It costs delayed decisions, because nobody wants to act on data that another department disputes. It costs trust, which is the hardest loss to recover: after a few meetings like that, every new number arrives with the question “but whose number is this?” And it costs rework, because each department starts keeping its own dashboard, its own spreadsheet and its own calculation, partly to protect itself in the next argument.
The end result is an odd one. The company invests in systems, dashboards and reports to make better decisions, and ends up making them more slowly.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
text:
Nobody was wrong
The most important detail in the scene is that all three numbers were right. Each department started from a reasonable choice for its own work: what counts as an absence, whether long-term absences are included, whether the base is scheduled hours or days worked, which people belong in the denominator. HR was looking at people’s health, Operations at team coverage, Finance at cost.
The problem was not the math. It was the lack of three things: an official definition, a person responsible for it and a rule for changing it. Without them, each department fills the gap its own way, and every one of them has good arguments.
That is why the fix is rarely technical. A new dashboard, prettier or faster, just shows the same three versions in more colors.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
section: What KPI governance looks like in practice
text:
What KPI governance looks like in practice
The word governance scares people, because it brings to mind committees, policies and documents nobody reads. In practice, for KPIs, it comes down to a few pieces.
The first is a definition sheet for each KPI: what it measures, the formula, where the data comes from, how often it is updated and what the target is. One page per KPI is enough.
The second is an owner. Not the person who calculates the number, but the person who answers for the definition: they decide what goes in and what stays out, and they are the one others turn to when a question comes up.
The third is a version log. Definitions change, and they should when the business changes. What cannot happen is a change nobody knows about. Every change gets a version number, a date and a reason.
The fourth is a single place where the official definition lives. It can be a shared document, an intranet page or a tab in the dashboard itself. What matters is that, whenever a question comes up, everyone knows where to look.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
text:
What changes afterward
In the case, leadership asked for a full inventory at the end of the year. It found 40 KPIs in use, scattered across dashboards, spreadsheets and presentations. Only 13 had a definition clear enough for two people to arrive at the same number.
After the review, 14 stayed as leadership KPIs, 14 moved to the department level, 6 were merged because they measured the same thing under different names and 6 were discontinued because nobody used them to decide anything. The first version of the definition sheets came out in January, and the first revisions followed in the months after, already on record.
The company started looking at fewer numbers, and talking more about what they said.

title: When every department calculates the same KPI its own way
text:
How to start tomorrow
You do not need a big project to take the first step. Three moves are enough to change the mood of the meetings.
First, list the KPIs that exist today: name, where each one appears, who calculates it and what it is used for. The list is usually longer than anyone expects, and simply having it already exposes duplicates.
Second, write the definition sheet for the ten most used KPIs in results meetings. You do not have to start with all of them. The ten that cause the most arguments are the ones that give back the most time once they are clear.
Third, agree on who can change a definition and how the change is recorded. A simple rule, approved by leadership, keeps the next version from being born quietly inside a spreadsheet.
After that, the dashboard goes back to doing its job: showing a number everyone trusts, so the meeting can be about what to do.

The full case, with the inventory of all 40 KPIs, the definition sheets and the three definitions calculated side by side, is in One number, three answers.
If the same KPI has more than one version at your company too, tell me how it works today. I will tell you where to start.

text:
The story
At the July 2025 results meeting, Vallora heard three absenteeism rates for June. HR showed 4.38%, Operations 3.54% and Finance 2.15%, and the meeting spent half an hour arguing about which one was right.










Absenteeism rate calculated each department’s way, from January 2024 to December 2025. The vertical line marks June 2025, the month discussed at the July meeting.















Absenteeism rate calculated each department’s way, from January 2024 to December 2025. The vertical line marks June 2025, the month discussed at the July meeting.





None of them was wrong. Each department calculated what it needed for its own work and gave the result the same name. The problem was not arithmetic, it was governance: nobody had written down what “absenteeism rate” meant at the company, or who got to decide.
The scene repeated itself over the following months, and in December leadership asked for an inventory of every KPI that circulated in the monthly presentations. Forty turned up, from six departments, and only 13 were well defined. The work took five weeks, in four stages:

Interviews with the people who produce the numbers and the people who use them, in all six departments.
Inventory and diagnosis of each KPI.
Definition sheets for the KPIs that go to leadership.
Governance rules: who proposes, who approves, how a change is recorded.

section: The divergence: three calculations, one name
text:
The divergence: three calculations, one name
The three rates come from the same data and answer different questions. The decision was to keep all three, each with its own name, and reserve “Absenteeism rate” for HR’s definition, which is the same as the Radar’s.

Operations. Operations counts the whole day even when the absence is a late arrival, which pushes the rate up, but takes anyone absent for more than 15 days off the schedule, which pulls it down. On balance, it lands a little below HR. In four of the 24 months (January and February 2024, September and November 2025), the balance flipped: in months with few long-term absences, counting the whole day weighs more, and Operations comes out above HR.
Finance. It leaves out unexcused absences and late arrivals that are docked from pay, and whatever INSS pays from day 16 of a leave. That is why it runs well below the other two. In Brazil, the employer pays the first 15 days of sick or injury leave; from day 16 on, the social security agency (INSS) pays.



Show the R code for the three definitions
# Tipos da base: 1 atestado médico, 2 consulta ou exame (parcial), 3 acidente
# de trabalho, 4 afastamento do INSS, 5 falta injustificada, 6 atraso ou saída
# antecipada, 7 licença legal (CLT art. 473), 8 acompanhamento de dependente,
# 9 licença maternidade/paternidade (dias já fora da jornada no Radar).
# RH: horas de ausência dos tipos que contam no Radar ÷ horas previstas.
rh <- ausencias |> filter(considera_taxa == 1)

# Operação: dias escalados com qualquer ausência (atraso ou saída antecipada só
# acima de 10 minutos) ÷ dias escalados. Quem está afastado há mais de 15 dias
# (do 16º dia de um evento longo em diante) sai da escala, no numerador e no
# denominador.
afastado <- ausencias |> filter(dias_corridos > 15, dia_do_evento > 15) |> distinct(id_funcionario, data)
escala <- jornada |> anti_join(afastado, c("id_funcionario", "data"))
dias_com_ausencia <- escala |>
  semi_join(filter(ausencias, id_tipo_ausencia != 6 | horas_ausencia * 60 > 10), c("id_funcionario", "data"))

# Financeiro: horas pagas pela empresa ÷ horas previstas. Entram atestados e
# acidentes de até 15 dias, consultas, licenças legais e os 15 primeiros dias
# dos afastamentos longos por doença ou acidente (tipos 1, 3 e 4), que a empresa
# paga por lei. Ficam fora faltas e atrasos (descontados), o que o INSS paga e
# o acompanhamento de dependente.
pagas <- ausencias |>
  filter(id_tipo_ausencia == 7 |
           (id_tipo_ausencia %in% c(1, 2, 3) & dias_corridos <= 15) |
           (id_tipo_ausencia %in% c(1, 3, 4) & dias_corridos > 15 & dia_do_evento <= 15))

text:
Results
The monthly meeting traded six presentations and 40 numbers for a single page with 14 KPIs, each with its owner in the room to explain it. When Operations talks about its rate, it now goes by another name, and the July argument does not happen again. The Absenteeism Radar now uses the official PES-01 definition.

title: One number, three answers: KPI governance at Vallora Logística
text:
What this case demonstrates

Separating the math from the governance. A divergence is rarely a calculation error; it is almost always the lack of a written definition and of someone who decides.
Cutting without deleting. Twenty-six KPIs left the leadership meeting, and no department lost information it needs.
Definition sheets that answer the questions that start arguments: what goes in, what stays out, whether higher is better, when the number closes.
Changes on record, so that today’s number stays comparable with last year’s.
A bridge to BI. The definition sheets become the DAX measures and the dashboard’s data dictionary, and the dashboard stops hiding rules.

title: Employee turnover in supermarkets: statistical consulting for an undergraduate thesis
text:
The request
A Business Administration student was finishing an undergraduate thesis titled Leadership, recognition and turnover intention among supermarket employees in central-western Minas Gerais. He ran a Google Forms survey in stores across the region: profile questions plus 20 statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), in five blocks.









Block
Items
Sample statement

“My supervisor treats me with respect.”


Recognition

4
“I can plan my days off in advance.”


Turnover intention
3
“I plan to look for another job in the next 12 months.”




The project had four hypotheses:

H1. Better-rated leadership reduces the intention to leave.
H2. More recognition reduces the intention to leave.
H3. Better-rated pay reduces the intention to leave, with a smaller effect than H1 and H2.
H4. Better work-life balance reduces the intention to leave.

He had the spreadsheet exported from Forms and his advisor’s instruction to “do the statistics part.” He needed to know what to run, in what order, how to check whether he could trust the results and how to report everything in the thesis.

What I did

1. Cleaning


Show the R code
bruto <- read_csv("dados/respostas_brutas.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dic <- read_csv("dados/dicionario.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# O Forms exporta o texto inteiro da pergunta como nome da coluna;
# o dicionário troca cada um por um código curto (LID1, REC2...).
names(bruto) <- dic$codigo[match(names(bruto), dic$coluna)]
itens <- filter(dic, construto != "Perfil") |>
  mutate(enunciado = str_match(coluna, "\\[(.*)\\]$")[, 2])
cod <- itens$codigo
blocos <- split(cod, substr(cod, 1, 3))

brancos <- function(df) rowSums(is.na(select(df, all_of(cod))))
iguais <- function(df) apply(select(df, all_of(cod)), 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE) == 0

passo1 <- filter(bruto, aceite == "Sim")
passo2 <- filter(passo1, brancos(passo1) <= 4)      # até 20% dos 20 itens em branco
passo3 <- filter(passo2, !iguais(passo2))           # mesma resposta nos 20 itens

excluidas <- c(sem_aceite = nrow(bruto) - nrow(passo1), brancos = nrow(passo1) - nrow(passo2),
               iguais = nrow(passo2) - nrow(passo3))
celulas_brancas <- sum(is.na(select(passo3, all_of(cod))))

3. Scale reliability
Before adding statements up into a score, you have to show that they measure the same thing. I used two indicators: Cronbach’s alpha, which the advisor and the thesis committee expect to see, and McDonald’s omega, which is better suited when the statements do not all carry the same weight in the construct. Above .70 is the usual threshold.


Show the R code
confiab <- function(cols) {
  x <- select(d, all_of(cols))
  c(alfa = suppressWarnings(psych::alpha(x)$total$raw_alpha),
    omega = suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(psych::omega(x, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)))
}
rem_sem4 <- c("REM1", "REM2", "REM3")

  lapply(names(blocos), function(b) c(bloco = b, itens = length(blocos[[b]]), confiab(blocos[[b]]))),
  c(bloco = "REM_sem4", itens = 3, confiab(rem_sem4))
) |>
  mutate(across(c(itens, alfa, omega), as.numeric)) |>
  arrange(match(bloco, c("LID", "REC", "REM", "REM_sem4", "EQU", "INT")))

Perceived pay came in at .68 because of one item: “I receive my transportation allowance on time” (REM4) barely moves with the other three (a correlation of .09 with their total, against .58 or more for the rest). That makes sense: it measures whether a benefit arrives on time, not whether the pay feels fair. Without it, alpha rises to .82. 4. Exploratory factor analysis
Factor analysis checks whether the 20 statements group into the five blocks the questionnaire intended. Because the answers are ordinal (1 to 5), I used polychoric correlation, which treats each answer as a band on an underlying continuous scale and does not assume that the distance between “1” and “2” equals the distance between “4” and “5”.

x_itens <- select(d, all_of(cod))

# Dá a cada fator o código do bloco cujos itens carregam mais nele.
dominante <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(cargas)), function(f) {
  names(which.max(tapply(abs(cargas[, f]), substr(rownames(cargas), 1, 3), mean)))
})
colnames(cargas) <- dominante
cargas <- cargas[, c("LID", "REC", "REM", "EQU", "INT")]
carga_rem4 <- max(abs(cargas["REM4", ]))

Likert scale scores tend to be skewed and full of ties, so I compared the intention to leave across groups with non-parametric tests, always reporting the effect size, which tells you whether a difference is large or merely statistically detectable.

7. Multiple regression
Correlation looks at one factor at a time. To test the hypotheses, the question is different: how much does each factor matter when the others are in the same model? I used multiple linear regression with the four scores standardized (so the effects are comparable) and three controls: night shift, up to 1 year of tenure and sex.


Show the R code
dm <- d |>
  transmute(INT = INT, LID = LID, REC = REC, REM = REM, EQU = EQU,
            noturno = as.numeric(turno == "Noite"),
            novato = as.numeric(tempo_casa == "Até 1 ano"),
            feminino = as.numeric(sexo == "Feminino")) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(across(c(INT, LID, REC, REM, EQU), \(v) as.numeric(scale(v))))
modelo <- lm(INT ~ LID + REC + REM + EQU + noturno + novato + feminino, data = dm)

# Pressupostos
vifs <- vif(modelo)
bp <- bptest(modelo)
sw <- shapiro.test(residuals(modelo))
cook_max <- max(cooks.distance(modelo))

# Erros-padrão robustos (HC3): protegem os testes se a variância dos resíduos não for constante.
v_hc3 <- vcovHC(modelo, type = "HC3")
rob <- coeftest(modelo, vcov. = v_hc3)
ic <- coefci(modelo, vcov. = v_hc3)
resultado <- tibble(termo = rownames(rob), beta = rob[, 1], ep = rob[, 2], p = rob[, 4],
                    li = ic[, 1], ls = ic[, 2]) |>
  filter(termo != "(Intercept)")
ajuste <- summary(modelo)
# H3 diz que o efeito da remuneração é menor: testa se os coeficientes são iguais.
igual_lid <- linearHypothesis(modelo, "REM = LID", vcov. = v_hc3)
igual_rec <- linearHypothesis(modelo, "REM = REC", vcov. = v_hc3)
teste <- function(h) c(F = h$F[2], gl1 = h$Df[2], gl2 = h$Res.Df[2], p = h$`Pr(>F)`[2])
menor_confirmado <- igual_lid$`Pr(>F)`[2] < 0.05 && igual_rec$`Pr(>F)`[2] < 0.05
# O texto das páginas foi escrito para o caso em que a diferença não se confirma.
stopifnot(!menor_confirmado)

# H3 tem duas partes: reduz (testada pelo β) e com efeito menor (testada acima).
hipoteses <- tibble(termo = c("LID", "REC", "REM", "EQU")) |>
  left_join(resultado, by = "termo") |>
  mutate(decisao = case_when(!(beta < 0 & p < 0.05) ~ "nao",
                             termo == "REM" & !menor_confirmado ~ "parcial",
                             TRUE ~ "sim"))


Before reading the coefficients, I checked the assumptions:

Multicollinearity: highest VIF of 1.47, well below the usual limit of 5. The blocks are correlated, but not to the point of being confounded.
Residual variance: Breusch-Pagan test, p = .713. No strong sign of non-constant variance; even so, the tests use robust standard errors (HC3), which cost little and protect the result.
Normality of residuals: Shapiro-Wilk, p = .049. With more than 200 cases, a slight departure does not compromise the coefficient tests.
Influential cases: highest Cook’s distance of 0.04, far below 1. No single response changes the result.

The model explains 43% of the variation in the intention to leave (adjusted R² = .41, N = 210).
H3 says the effect of pay is smaller than those of leadership and recognition. Looking at the βs is not enough: you have to test whether the difference between them is real. The test of equality of coefficients (with the same HC3 correction) did not confirm the difference: F(1, 202) = 3.02, p = .084 against leadership and F(1, 202) = 1.92, p = .167 against recognition.

grafico_likert <- function(res, tx) {
  enunciados <- if (is.null(tx$enunciados)) setNames(res$itens$enunciado, res$itens$codigo) else tx$enunciados
  cod <- res$itens$codigo
  inv <- if_else(res$itens$invertido == "sim", paste0(" (", tx$invertido, ")"), "")
  rotulos_itens <- setNames(paste0(cod, inv, ": ", enunciados[cod]), cod)
  cores_likert <- setNames(c("#6a4fa3", "#b9aee0", "#d9dbe1", "#9dbde8", cor[["azul"]]), tx$likert)

  # Barras divergentes: a resposta neutra fica metade de cada lado do zero.
  lik <- res$respostas |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "codigo", values_to = "resposta") |>
    drop_na() |>
    count(codigo, resposta) |>
    group_by(codigo) |>
    complete(resposta = 1:5, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
    arrange(resposta, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(p = n / sum(n),
           inicio = -(p[1] + p[2] + p[3] / 2) + lag(cumsum(p), default = 0),
           fim = inicio + p, meio = (inicio + fim) / 2) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(nivel = factor(tx$likert[resposta], tx$likert),
           bloco = factor(tx$blocos[substr(codigo, 1, 3)], tx$blocos),
           item = factor(rotulos_itens[codigo], rev(rotulos_itens)))
  totais <- lik |>
    group_by(item, bloco) |>
    summarise(discorda = sum(p[resposta <= 2]), concorda = sum(p[resposta >= 4]), .groups = "drop")
  rotulados <- filter(lik, p >= 0.12)

    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.92, 0.92), breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), labels = \(x) tx$pct(abs(x))) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = label_wrap_gen(40)) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, override.aes = list(linewidth = 4))) +

Pay is the lowest-rated area. REM4 stands apart from the other three items in its block, the same pattern that the reliability analysis and the factor analysis pointed to.

To test the hypotheses, a multiple linear regression with robust standard errors (HC3) was estimated, with turnover intention as the dependent variable. The model explained 43% of the variance (adjusted R² = .41). Perceived leadership (β = −0.31, p < .001) and recognition (β = −0.30, p < .001) were negatively associated with turnover intention, supporting H1 and H2.
